title: The canopy
hook: the wedding canopy is a new home, open on every side like Abraham's tent
carry: a house open on all sides

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tena'im, and your line was conditions: terms said out loud before the building starts. Today, the building itself, and it has no walls.

A pole at each corner. A cloth across the top. That's all. No walls, no door, no lock. Sometimes the cloth is a prayer shawl that belonged to a grandparent; sometimes it's embroidered, plain white, or a quilt friends stitched together. At some weddings, friends hold the poles by hand, and you can see their arms get tired. The couple walks in, and the wind comes straight through. This little shelter is where a Jewish wedding happens. Why would a wedding happen in a room you can't close?
screen: `A POLE AT EACH CORNER, ONE CLOTH.` → `NO WALLS, NO DOOR.` → `WHY A ROOM YOU CAN'T CLOSE?`

segments.voice: Start with the word. In Psalm nineteen, the sun rises like a groom. The King James puts it: "as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber." The Hebrew for that chamber is a form of chuppah. In the Bible it's a wedding room; at a Jewish wedding it has shrunk to a cloth on poles, and kept its meaning. The couple stands under it together, and tradition treats the chuppah as their first shared home, before there's a lease or a key. Being brought under it is part of what makes them married. Now the open sides. You met Abraham at his tent back in your first year, sitting "in the tent door in the heat of the day," then running to meet strangers with water for their feet and bread. The midrash adds a detail the verse doesn't: his tent had openings on every side, so travelers from any direction found a door facing them. The chuppah, some teachers say, carries that tent into every wedding. A Jewish home is meant to be open to guests from its very first minute. And what holds it up? Only cloth; a gust can lift it. When friends hold the poles, the picture is plain: a new home stands because the people around it keep it standing. A house open on all sides needs, and welcomes, everyone nearby.
screen: `A WEDDING ROOM IN THE PSALMS.` · `THE COUPLE'S FIRST HOME.` · `ABRAHAM'S TENT, OPEN EVERY WAY.` · `HELD UP BY FRIENDS.` · then, large: `A HOUSE OPEN ON ALL SIDES.`

segments.voice: If you can, move under a doorway, a tree, a porch roof, or the open sky; if not, look up, then toward the nearest window. Let your home come to mind as it is right now, and ask: if every side had a door, who would walk in, and who could, if you opened one more side? Let one name come, and hold it gently.
Chuppah: the wedding canopy. A first home, with a roof and no walls, open like Abraham's tent. Today's word.
Your line: a house open on all sides. The door faces every direction. That's day one thousand three hundred five.

chat.says: Why do Jewish couples get married under a canopy with no walls?
options: It's their first home, open on all sides like Abraham's tent, for guests.
It's just for shade; outdoor weddings needed cover from sun and rain.
The open sides show the marriage can be left easily if it fails.
chat.meaning: Tradition treats the chuppah as the couple's first home; some teachers link its open sides to Abraham's tent, open to guests from every direction.
